evidence.title: Efficiency of Six Dairy and Dual-Purpose Cattle Breeds Reared in Low- and High-Productivity Mountain Farming Systems
evidence.abstract: Breed and herd are major determinants of milk productivity and efficiency. This study evaluated 1508 lactating cows from three dairy (Holstein, Brown Swiss, Jersey) and three dual-purpose (Simmental, Rendena, Alpine Grey) breeds across 41 multi-breed mountain herds. Data on body size, production, and milk samples were collected. Daily milk yield, milk energy, and cheese yield were quantified, and herds were classified under high (>75 MJ/d) or low (<75 MJ/d) average daily milk energy production. Cheese-making traits were predicted from 508 individual model cheese-making trials. Nine productivity ratios and three efficiency indicators (energy efficiency, economic efficiency, and income over feed costs) were calculated. Data was analyzed using mixed models including herd productivity class, herd within class (random), breed, parity, and days in milk. Differences among breeds were smaller within herds than across herds and were more pronounced for quality and cheese-making traits. Dairy and dual-purpose breeds showed similar overall performance. Jerseys were the least productive in absolute terms but, when adjusted for body size, were as or more efficient than other dairy breeds. Holsteins had the highest milk yield, whereas Brown Swiss showed superior milk quality and cheese yield. Simmental outperformed local dual-purpose breeds in size and production but not in efficiency. Accurate assessment of energy and economic efficiency is essential for breeding and crossbreeding strategies.

evidence.title: Characterization of premium soft ice creams produced from Jersey and Holstein milk
evidence.abstract: This study compared the physicochemical, structural, and antioxidant properties of premium soft ice creams (14–16% fat) made from Jersey milk (JIC) and Holstein milk (HIC). Both JIC and HIC were successfully formulated with over 14% fat content. Although most nutritional components showed no significant differences, JIC contained a higher level of saturated fat. Despite the lower viscosity of the Jersey milk mix (JM), and similar overrun values in both samples, JIC exhibited a slower melting rate, greater melting resistance, and larger, more irregular air cells than HIC. Color analysis revealed an increase in lightness after freezing, with JIC maintaining a relatively darker tone. Antioxidant activity, as assessed by the ABTS assay, was higher in casein isolates from Jersey milk; however, this trend was reversed in the final ice cream products, likely due to protein modifications and the formation of Maillard reaction products during processing. Overall, the results suggest that Jersey milk contributes to improved melting resistance and structural quality, making it a suitable raw material for producing high-fat premium ice cream.

evidence.title: Effect of blending Jersey and Holstein-Friesian milk on Cheddar cheese processing, composition, and quality.
evidence.abstract: The effect of Jersey milk use solely or at different inclusion rates in Holstein-Friesian milk on Cheddar cheese production was investigated. Cheese was produced every month over a year using nonstandardized milk consisting of 0, 25, 50, 75, and 100% Jersey milk in Holstein-Friesian milk in a 100-L vat. Actual, theoretical, and moisture-adjusted yield increased linearly with percentage of Jersey milk. This was also associated with increased fat and protein recoveries and lower yield of whey. The composition of whey was also affected by the percentage of Jersey milk, with lower whey protein and higher whey lactose and solids. Cutting time was lower when Jersey milk was used, but the cutting to milling time was higher because of slower acidity development. Hence, overall cheesemaking time was not affected by the use of Jersey milk. Using Jersey milk increased cheese fat content in autumn, winter, and spring and decreased cheese moisture in spring and summer. Cheese protein, salt, and pH levels were not affected. Cheese was analyzed for texture and color, and it was professionally graded at 3 and 8mo. The effect of Jersey on cheese sensory quality was an increase in cheese yellowness during summer and a higher total grading score at 3mo in winter; no other difference in cheese quality was found. The study indicates that using Jersey milk is a valid method of improving Cheddar cheese yield.

abstract.value:
Photovoltaic Concentrator systems, which increase the solar radiation intensity on the

photovoltaic cells, may reduce the system cost, if the cost of the concentrator is less than

the photovoltaic material displaced. An Asymmetric Compound Parabolic Photovoltaic

Concentrator (ACPPVC) for building façade integration with a solar concentration ratio of

2.0 has been designed, fabricated and experimentally characterised. The truncated

ACPPVC has acceptance half angles of 0° and 55° and an absorber width of 125mm. Phase

Change Materials (PCM) have been integrated to the rear of the PV panel to moderate the

temperature rise of the PV and maintain good solar-electrical conversion efficiency. The

thermal behaviour of a Fresnel lens PV Concentrator (FPVC) has also been studied in this

work.

A two-dimensional ray trace technique has been used to predict the optical performance

and the angular acceptance of the ACPPVC system. The predicted highest optical

efficiency was 88.67% for the ACPPVC-55 system. Extensive indoor experimental

characterisation of a number of PV systems was undertaken for a range of incident solar

radiation intensities using a highly collimated solar simulator developed specifically for this

project. Experimental results showed that the electrical output from the ACPPVC-55 was

approximately 1.8 of that of a non-concentrating PV system with similar solar cells area.

The electrical conversion efficiency for the ACPPVC-55 system was further increased,

when RT27 PCM was incorporated to its rear

candidates.mechanism: A phase-change thermal mass (PCM) placed at the rear of a heat-generating component absorbs incident thermal flux through latent heat storage, buffering temperature rise of the active component and preserving its functional efficiency.
candidates.intervention: Integrate a paraffin-based phase change material (RT27-class) pad or encapsulated module to the rear of the electric power steering (EPS) control unit/heat-sink path of the 2020 Honda Civic, so that heat generated by the EPS power module during sustained 65 MPH driving is absorbed by the PCM via melting rather than conducted to the EPS motor windings and coolant loop alone.

evidence_bundle.mechanism_source_span: Phase Change Materials (PCM) have been integrated to the rear of the PV panel to moderate the temperature rise of the PV and maintain good solar-electrical conversion efficiency. The electrical conversion efficiency for the ACPPVC-55 system was further increased, when RT27 PCM was incorporated to its rear

constraint_set.problem_constraint: must diagnose intermittent steering and overheating in 2020 Honda Civic
constraint_set.boundary_conditions: Mechanism active when ambient plus EPS heat-flux drives the PCM through its phase-transition band (approx. 25–30 °C) and EPS duty cycle remains within cruise to moderate-load envelope; ineffective if EPS heat generation rate exceeds PCM absorption rate at >90 °C case temperatures or if vehicle is operated continuously at standstill with steering locked.

known_failure_modes: PCM encapsulation rupture under vibration releases paraffin onto EPS electronics

warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Breed and herd are major determinants of milk productivity and efficiency. This study evaluated 1508 lactating cows from three dairy (Holstein, Brown Swiss, Jersey) and three dual-purpose (Simmental, Rendena, Alpine Grey) breeds across 41 multi-breed mountain herds. Data on body size, production, and milk samples were collected. Daily milk yield, milk energy, and cheese yield were quantified, and herds were classified under high (>75 MJ/d) or low (<75 MJ/d) average daily milk energy production. Cheese-making traits were predicted from 508 individual model cheese-making trials. Nine productivity ratios and three efficiency indicators (energy efficiency, economic efficiency, and income over feed costs) were calculated. Data was analyzed using mixed models including herd productivity class, herd within class (random), breed, parity, and days in milk. Differences among breeds were smaller within herds than across herds and were more pronounced for quality and cheese-making traits. Dairy and dual-purpose breeds showed similar overall performance. Jerseys were the least productive in absolute terms but, when adjusted for body size, were as or more efficient than other dairy breeds. Holsteins had the highest milk yield, whereas Brown Swiss showed superior milk quality and cheese yield. Simmental outperformed local dual-purpose breeds in size and production but not in efficiency. Accurate assessment of energy and economic efficiency is essential for breeding and crossbreeding strategies.

custody_records.raw_content: This study compared the physicochemical, structural, and antioxidant properties of premium soft ice creams (14–16% fat) made from Jersey milk (JIC) and Holstein milk (HIC). Both JIC and HIC were successfully formulated with over 14% fat content. Although most nutritional components showed no significant differences, JIC contained a higher level of saturated fat. Despite the lower viscosity of the Jersey milk mix (JM), and similar overrun values in both samples, JIC exhibited a slower melting rate, greater melting resistance, and larger, more irregular air cells than HIC. Color analysis revealed an increase in lightness after freezing, with JIC maintaining a relatively darker tone. Antioxidant activity, as assessed by the ABTS assay, was higher in casein isolates from Jersey milk; however, this trend was reversed in the final ice cream products, likely due to protein modifications and the formation of Maillard reaction products during processing. Overall, the results suggest that Jersey milk contributes to improved melting resistance and structural quality, making it a suitable raw material for producing high-fat premium ice cream.

custody_records.raw_content: The effect of Jersey milk use solely or at different inclusion rates in Holstein-Friesian milk on Cheddar cheese production was investigated. Cheese was produced every month over a year using nonstandardized milk consisting of 0, 25, 50, 75, and 100% Jersey milk in Holstein-Friesian milk in a 100-L vat. Actual, theoretical, and moisture-adjusted yield increased linearly with percentage of Jersey milk. This was also associated with increased fat and protein recoveries and lower yield of whey. The composition of whey was also affected by the percentage of Jersey milk, with lower whey protein and higher whey lactose and solids. Cutting time was lower when Jersey milk was used, but the cutting to milling time was higher because of slower acidity development. Hence, overall cheesemaking time was not affected by the use of Jersey milk. Using Jersey milk increased cheese fat content in autumn, winter, and spring and decreased cheese moisture in spring and summer. Cheese protein, salt, and pH levels were not affected. Cheese was analyzed for texture and color, and it was professionally graded at 3 and 8mo. The effect of Jersey on cheese sensory quality was an increase in cheese yellowness during summer and a higher total grading score at 3mo in winter; no other difference in cheese quality was found. The study indicates that using Jersey milk is a valid method of improving Cheddar cheese yield.

Photovoltaic Concentrator systems, which increase the solar radiation intensity on the

photovoltaic cells, may reduce the system cost, if the cost of the concentrator is less than

the photovoltaic material displaced. An Asymmetric Compound Parabolic Photovoltaic

Concentrator (ACPPVC) for building façade integration with a solar concentration ratio of

2.0 has been designed, fabricated and experimentally characterised. The truncated

ACPPVC has acceptance half angles of 0° and 55° and an absorber width of 125mm. Phase

Change Materials (PCM) have been integrated to the rear of the PV panel to moderate the

temperature rise of the PV and maintain good solar-electrical conversion efficiency. The

thermal behaviour of a Fresnel lens PV Concentrator (FPVC) has also been studied in this

work.

A two-dimensional ray trace technique has been used to predict the optical performance

and the angular acceptance of the ACPPVC system. The predicted highest optical

efficiency was 88.67% for the ACPPVC-55 system. Extensive indoor experimental

characterisation of a number of PV systems was undertaken for a range of incident solar

radiation intensities using a highly collimated solar simulator developed specifically for this

project. Experimental results showed that the electrical output from the ACPPVC-55 was

approximately 1.8 of that of a non-concentrating PV system with similar solar cells area.

The electrical conversion efficiency for the ACPPVC-55 system was further increased,

when RT27 PCM was incorporated to its rear

custody_records.raw_content: Different heating system controllers for passive solar buildings are compared on two different buildings.The performance criterion combines energy performance and thermal comfort using the "costfunction" paradigm. The experimental facilities did not allow a direct experimental comparison by using two identical buildings. The controllers were implemented alternatively in one building and a performance comparison was obtained in two ways: first by identifying short periods that have similar driving variables (weather conditions and building occupancy) and comparing the experimental results obtained in both cases. The second method mixes experiments and simulation using a well-tuned model of the building and its occupants. This paper discusses the results obtained using the above methods and shows that both methods give consistent estimates of the difference between controllers, while the second method allows to extrapolate useful information from the limited data available
